title: Origen's search
hook: a brilliant, controversial teacher who read scripture as a journey upward

segments.voice: Yesterday, Irenaeus against contempt for matter: creation called very good, bread from the earth. Your line was matter matters. What did you do for your body? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

Read the first chapter of Genesis slowly and something odd turns up. "And the evening and the morning were the first day." Then a second day. Then a third. Evenings and mornings, one after another. And only on the fourth day does God make the sun. In Alexandria, a teacher named Origen noticed exactly this, and pointed it out to his readers. He didn't close the book. He didn't pretend not to see it. He took it as a signal: keep going, there's more here than the surface. Today, Origen's search.

Origen gave his students a picture. A human being, he said, is body, soul and spirit, and so is scripture. Paul uses those three words together: "your whole spirit and soul and body." The body of scripture is its plain sense, the story as it stands, and Origen held that it feeds many readers well. The soul is what the text asks of your life. The spirit is where it points: toward Christ and toward God. So reading becomes a climb, from the words, through your life, up toward God. He leaned on Paul again: "the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life." He was brilliant, and he was controversial, then and later. Some of his bolder guesses, about where souls come from and how all things end, were condemned long after he died. Others honor him as a giant of Christian learning. Christians still argue about how to read him, and this path won't settle it. Tradition says he suffered in a persecution for his faith. Here's what his search looks like on the road. In Luke, two disciples walk to Emmaus with a stranger who opens the scriptures to them. Only later do they recognize the risen Jesus. Afterward they say: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" That's reading upward. And look back at this week's road. A friend as the third in the room. Thanks in every thing. A holy laugh. Love gathering up the law. Seeds of truth. Matter that matters. And now a search that keeps climbing.
screen: `THE LETTER KILLETH, THE SPIRIT GIVETH LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse for its journey. Settle, and breathe. Take one line, from the Psalms: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." First, the body: what does it say? A shepherd, a sheep, enough. Then the soul: what does it ask of your life today? Maybe to stop grabbing. Then the spirit: where does it point? Let it lead you upward, as far as it will go. If you pray, you can rest in the line itself. If not, just let each layer have a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Origen's search. A teacher who read scripture as a climb, from its plain sense, through the life of the reader, up toward God.
Your line: read upward. Today, carry your verse with you, and come back to it once to ask the next question. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians read scripture for its plain sense and for deeper meanings; spiritual reading such as lectio divina moves slowly from what a text says to what it asks and to prayer, and preachers draw out both history and meaning.

pairs: what it asks of your life

fork.setup: you're reading Genesis 1 and notice evenings and mornings before the sun exists. what do you do?
options: close the book. it can't be right.
keep reading, and look for a deeper sense.
fork.reveal: Origen pointed out the puzzle himself and took it as a signal to read for a spiritual meaning, climbing from the letter toward God.

trapdoor: what you thought: reading the Bible means taking every line at face value, or else explaining it away.
what it means: Origen read in layers: body, soul and spirit, the plain story, its claim on your life, and where it points.
what a scholar hears: Origen's On First Principles lays out the threefold sense and names the Genesis days without a sun as a puzzle.

Origen paraphrased: threefold sense of scripture (body, soul, spirit) from On First Principles 4.2.4, with his appeal to the human person; the Genesis days-without-sun puzzle from 4.3.1. Confirm references.
Origen's use of 2 Corinthians 3:6 is stated as 'He leaned on Paul'; confirm he cites it in this connection.

Controversy: 'some of his bolder guesses, about where souls come from and how all things end, were condemned long after he died' refers to the sixth-century condemnations of Origenism (pre-existence of souls, apokatastasis); no date given. Confirm fair; note these concerned ideas attributed to him, sometimes via later Origenists.
'Tradition says he suffered in a persecution' (Eusebius, Church History 6.39 on the Decian persecution); confirm.
Practice and soul-layer gloss 'maybe to stop grabbing' is an example, not a claim about the text; confirm tone.
Original left null: no single Greek term chosen with certainty.

Audit pass: the Emmaus stranger is now identified as the risen Jesus, as Luke 24 does; leaving him only "a stranger" misread the passage. Origen's persecution is recorded by Eusebius (Church History 6.39), not only by tradition; wording kept cautious.
